html:
The Korean alphabet, Hangul, was created in 1443 under King Sejong the Great of Joseon and made public in 1446 in a book called Hunminjeongeum, "The Correct Sounds for the Instruction of the People".

Before this Koreans wrote in Chinese characters, which took years to learn and fit the Korean language badly. Sejong wrote that he pitied common people who could not set down their thoughts. The new script was simple enough to learn in days.

It is one of the few writing systems whose design is recorded. The basic consonant shapes picture the mouth, tongue and throat as they make each sound. The vowels are built from a dot and lines standing for heaven, earth and humankind. Letters are grouped into square syllable blocks.

Many scholars scorned it, and one king banned it in 1504. Elites kept using Chinese for centuries, while women, commoners and popular fiction used Hangul. It became the official script only in the Gabo Reform of the 1890s. Today it is the writing of both Koreas.
sum: The Korean alphabet, Hangul, was created in 1443 under King Sejong the Great of Joseon and made public in 1446 in a book called Hunminjeongeum, "The Correct Sounds for the Instruction of the People".
